opus-5.5.text:
I think what's exciting is that a lot of people who spend hours every day working with these models develop a kind of folk knowledge. They'll say things like, "If you give the model a moment to think before answering, it does better," or "The model seems to plan ahead when it writes poetry," or "It's sort of doing the math in a weird way, not the way it tells you it is." For a long time those were just vibes. You couldn't really check them, and you'd get these debates where one camp says the model is just predicting the next token and another camp says no, there's clearly something more going on.

With circuit tracing, we can actually open the model up on a specific prompt and look at the intermediate steps. And sometimes what we find is, oh, that intuition was right, and here's the mechanism. The rhyming example is a good one. When the model writes a couplet, we can see it picking out the rhyme word for the end of the next line before it starts writing that line, and then building the line to land there. People who'd played with the models a lot kind of suspected that, but now you can point to the features and even intervene on them. If you swap out the planned word, the model rewrites the line to hit the new target.

What I find really satisfying is that it turns an intuition into something you can work with. Once you know the mechanism, you can ask sharper questions. How far ahead does it plan? When does that break down? Is this the same circuit it uses in other settings? And it cuts both ways. Sometimes the intuition is confirmed, and sometimes we find the model is doing something quite different from what it says it's doing, like with arithmetic, where its explanation of carrying the one doesn't match the parallel, approximate-plus-precise pathways we actually see inside. Both outcomes are valuable, because they give people who rely on these models a more grounded picture of what's really going on, instead of just trusting their gut or trusting the model's own account of itself.

r001.rationale: The response says circuit tracing can reveal mechanisms behind users’ intuitions, but it does not state that a hint misleads an LLM or identify the causal mechanism by which that happens.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so one of the things I find really satisfying is that a lot of what we see in the circuits lines up with what people who use these models every day already suspected. If you've spent a lot of time prompting a model, you develop these folk theories about how it works. You notice that if you tell it to answer in French, it still seems to be "thinking" in roughly the same way it would in English, and just translating at the end. Or you notice that when it writes a poem, it seems to already know where the rhyme is going before it gets there. Or that when it does mental math, it seems to have a rough sense of the answer before it nails down the exact digits.

And for a long time, those were just intuitions. You couldn't really check them. The model is this giant pile of matrix multiplications, and the only evidence you had was behavioral. So people would argue about it. Someone would say, "it's just predicting the next token, there's no planning," and someone else would say, "well, it sure acts like it's planning," and there was no way to resolve that.

What's exciting about the circuit tracing work is that we can now actually open the model up and look. And in a bunch of these cases, the intuition turns out to be right, in a surprisingly literal way. With the rhyming example, you can find features that represent the candidate rhyme word firing at the start of the line, well before the model gets there, and if you intervene on them, the model rewrites the line to land on a different word. With the multilingual stuff, you can see shared, language-agnostic features in the middle of the network that get used regardless of whether the input was English, French, or Chinese. That's a mechanism, not a vibe.

I think there are two reasons that's exciting. The first is just validation of the method. If you build an interpretability tool and it only ever tells you surprising things, you should be a little nervous, because maybe your tool is making things up. When it confirms things that experienced practitioners independently arrived at, that's evidence the tool is actually seeing something real about the model.

The second is that it gives those intuitions teeth. Once you've seen the mechanism, you can start to ask much sharper questions. Not just "does the model plan ahead" but "where does it plan, how far ahead, what breaks it, and does the same circuit show up in cases where the model gets things wrong." And that last part is the one I really care about, because the same tools that confirm the comfortable intuitions also show you the cases where the model's explanation of what it did doesn't match what actually happened internally. So confirming the intuitions is kind of the entry fee. It's how you earn the trust to say something people won't like.

r001.rationale: The response says circuit tracing can confirm intuitions about rhyme and multilingual processing, but it does not describe a hint misleading an LLM or identify the causal mechanism by which that happens.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that we can start turning intuitions about model behavior into hypotheses we can actually test. If you’ve used these models a lot, you develop a sense of what they’re good at, where they struggle, and what might be happening underneath. But you’re still inferring all of that from inputs and outputs.

With circuit tracing, we can look inside and ask, “Is the model actually doing something like what we thought?” And even when the answer is yes, that’s valuable. It gives us more confidence in the method, and it lets us refine the intuition: which parts were right, which parts were incomplete, and under what circumstances does this explanation hold?

The exciting next step is finding cases where the mechanism surprises us. We want to get beyond explaining behavior we already recognize and toward predicting behavior we haven’t seen yet.

r001.rationale: The response says circuit tracing can test and refine intuitions about model behavior, but it does not mention a misleading hint or identify the specific causal mechanism by which a hint misleads an LLM.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is that we can start turning those intuitions into something we can actually investigate. When you use these models a lot, you develop a sense that, in certain situations, they’re doing something more complicated than just recalling an answer. But looking at the output alone doesn’t tell you how they got there.

Circuit tracing gives us a way to look inside and find evidence for a particular mechanism. And even when that confirms something you suspected, it’s valuable because you can ask much more precise follow-up questions: When does that mechanism appear? When does it fail? Does the same thing happen on a different task?

So I don’t think the exciting part is just, “We were right.” It’s that we’re beginning to connect our experience of using these systems with a concrete understanding of how they work.

r001.rationale: The response says circuit tracing can reveal mechanisms behind model behavior and test users’ intuitions, but it never mentions a hint misleading an LLM or identifies how that hint causes the misdirection.
